title: The Blind Men
summary: Birbal retells the ancient parable of the blind men and the elephant to settle a bitter religious dispute in the imperial council.
full_text:
A heated theological dispute broke out in the Diwan-i-Khas between scholars of different faiths. Each scholar insisted that his own doctrine possessed the absolute, exclusive truth, shouting insults and accusing others of heresy.

Akbar was distressed by the intolerance: 'Birbal, how can learned men who seek the same Almighty be so blind to one another?'

Birbal requested permission to demonstrate a parable. He brought an elephant into the courtyard and summoned six blind men from the city.

Birbal asked each blind man to touch the beast and describe what an elephant was like.

The first blind man felt the broad, flat side of the elephant and said: 'An elephant is like a colossal, sturdy wall!'

The second felt the sharp, smooth tusk: 'No, an elephant is like a spear!'

The third felt the trunk: 'You are both wrong; an elephant is like a giant serpent!'

The fourth felt the leg: 'An elephant is like the trunk of a great tree!'

The fifth felt the ear: 'An elephant is like a giant fan!'

The sixth felt the tail: 'An elephant is like a rough piece of rope!'

The six blind men began shouting and beating each other with their walking sticks, each swearing his own perception was the sole truth.

Birbal turned to the arguing scholars:

'Behold, my lords! Each blind man touched a genuine part of the elephant, yet each was completely wrong about the whole beast!

'So it is with mortal men who grasp only one aspect of the Infinite Divine and condemn their brothers. God is greater than any single human doctrine. Peace begins when men open their hearts to the whole truth instead of fighting over the part they have touched.'

Ashamed of their pettiness, the scholars fell silent, and Akbar thanked Birbal for illuminating the court with the spirit of harmony.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Blind Men"?
options: Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
